Unclear (deck metadata)

The title slide names Jan Steinbrener, but the PDF's own metadata says "Introduction to the Study Robotics & Artificial Intelligence (Part 2)", author "Kyamakya, Kyandoghere". The deck was probably built from an older version by another member of the faculty. The content isn't affected; only the attribution is uncertain.

The big picture

This is the robotics half of the programme introduction. 1 Introduction to AI was the AI half. It answers "what is a robot, what is it for, how does it relate to AI, and where is robotics in your degree?". A robot is an automated machine defined by a closed loop: it senses its environment with sensors, computes/thinks about what to do, and acts on the environment with actuators, then senses the result and goes round again. Robots are used where tasks are dangerous, dirty, dull or difficult (4D), and they automate, augment, assist or work autonomously (4A), from factories and farms to cars, kitchens and care homes. Robotics and AI are different fields. Robotics is an engineering discipline that needs hardware and software, and AI is a software discipline. Their overlap is the artificially intelligent robot, which is what this degree is about. Robotics itself is interdisciplinary (mechanical, electrical/electronic, computers, control), and that is why the curriculum has its mix of physics, ICE, AI and lab modules. The deck ends with a tour of the robotics research groups at AAU.

Outline

  • What is a robot?
  • Why use robots?

  • Compare/relation between robotics and AI
  • TeWi: a robotics perspective
  • Q&A: chat or email to robotics-ai@aau.at

What is a robot?

  • A robot is a type of automated machine that can execute specific tasks with little or no human intervention and with speed and precision.
  • 3 things that define a robot: SENSE, COMPUTE, ACT.
  • 5 defining characteristics of a robot: INTELLIGENCE, SENSE PERCEPTION, DEXTERITY, POWER, INDEPENDENCE.

Further definitions on the slide:

  • Robots are typically defined as physical agents that perform a variety of tasks by manipulating the physical world.
  • A robot is a reprogrammable, multifunctional manipulator designed to move material, parts, tools or specialised devices through variable programmed motions for the performance of a variety of tasks.
  • (highlighted) "A robot is a machine that gathers information about its environment (senses) and uses that information (thinks) to follow instructions to do work (acts)."

Icon strip: ROBOT = Sense + Think + Act (eye, brain, moving figure).

Intuition: the loop, not the parts

A sensor turns something about the world into a signal the computer can read (a camera, a distance sensor, a wheel encoder). An actuator turns a command from the computer into physical action (a motor, a gripper, a valve). The definition is about the cycle that connects them: measure → decide → move → measure again to see what the move did. "Compute" on the bullet list and "Think" on the icons are the same step. The diagram makes it concrete: compare where I am (present state) with where I want to be (goals) and work out the command that closes the gap.

Why does a robot have to keep sensing instead of planning once and executing the plan?

Because neither the world nor the robot is perfect. Objects move, people walk in, wheels slip, motors overshoot. A plan worked out once from a single snapshot drifts away from reality with every step. If the robot measures again after each action, it sees the error ("I'm 3 cm left of where I meant to be") and corrects it on the next pass. This idea is called feedback. It is why the slide draws a closed circle, and it is the core of control engineering later in the degree.

Worked example: is it a robot? (checking sense, compute, act)

Apply the slide's three-part test to four machines.

  1. Robot vacuum. Sense: bump and cliff sensors, often a lidar or camera. Compute: decides where to drive next and which areas are already clean. Act: wheel motors and brushes. All three are present → robot.
  2. Washing machine. Act: drum motor. Sense: at most a water-level sensor and a door switch. Compute: a fixed timed programme that doesn't adapt to what it senses about the laundry. This is borderline. It is automated, but it scores very low on intelligence and perception, so it is not usually called a robot.
  3. Remote-controlled toy car. Act: yes. Sense and compute: no, a human makes every decision. It fails "little or no human intervention" → not a robot.
  4. Chatbot. Compute: yes. Sense and act in the physical world: no. It is AI without a body → not a robot (see Robotics vs AI below).
Common mistake: "a robot is a metal human"

Science fiction (C-3PO, the Terminator) makes us picture humanoids. None of the slide's definitions mention shape. They are about function: sense, compute and act with little human intervention. A welding arm, a self-driving truck and a farm drone are robots. A humanoid statue or an animatronic puppet replaying a fixed motion is not. The modern humanoids later in the deck are one kind of robot among many.

Connection

The robotics course gives two more dictionary definitions (Cambridge, Britannica) and the history of the word "robot" in 1 Introduction (Introduction to Robotics). The two halves of the loop have their own lectures there: 2 Sensors and 3 Actuators.

Why use robots?

  • Application in 4D environments

    • Dangerous
    • Dirty
    • Dull
    • Difficult

  • 4A tasks

    • Automation
    • Augmentation
    • Assistance
    • Autonomous

Pictures: a humanoid robot vacuuming a bedroom, a small robot arm painting on a canvas, a robotic vehicle at a burning aircraft.

Why are 4D tasks the natural place for robots?

Each "D" matches something a machine does better than a person, or something a person shouldn't have to do. Dangerous: a robot can be lost in a fire, a mine or a reactor without anyone being hurt. Dirty: sewers, waste and chemical exposure are harmful or unpleasant for people and harmless to a machine. Dull: a robot doesn't get bored or tired, so its millionth weld is as precise as its first ("speed and precision" in the definition). Difficult: some tasks need more force, precision or endurance than a human body has, or a place a human can't reach (Mars, the deep sea).

Intuition: the four A's are four levels of human involvement
  • Automation: the robot repeats a defined task instead of a person (a factory arm).
  • Augmentation: the robot makes a person stronger or more capable. The human stays in charge (the exoskeletons and prostheses on the application slides below).
  • Assistance: the robot helps a person with a task (the social robots for children and elderly people below).
  • Autonomous: the robot decides and acts on its own in an open environment (self-driving cars and trucks below).

From automation to autonomy the robot needs more and more of the sense–think part of the loop, which is where AI comes in.

Application areas of robots

Diagram "Applications of AI Robots": robotic vehicles · industrial · construction · security · entertainment · customer service · logistics · agriculture · food processing · telepresence.

Connection

The group project in this course (0 Course Organisation – Program Introduction) asks you to "dream big" about a future robotics- or AI-driven product. The 4D/4A lists and this diagram are a ready-made checklist for finding and motivating an idea.

Examples of robots

Robots from science fiction

  • Talos by Hephaestus (Greek myth: a giant bronze guardian)
  • HAL 9000 (2001: A Space Odyssey)
  • C-3PO and R2-D2 (Star Wars)

First real robots

  • Shakey (1966–1972), Stanford Research Institute.
  • WABOT-1 (1967–1973), Waseda University, Japan: the first full-scale, intelligent humanoid robot. (Source on the slide: https://www.humanoid.waseda.ac.jp/booklet/kato_2.html.)
Connection: Shakey and the AI lecture

Shakey was the first mobile robot that reasoned about its own actions. It had a camera and bump sensors, a planner that worked out a sequence of steps to reach a goal, and wheels to carry the steps out: a full sense–think–act loop, in 1966. Its "think" part was symbolic AI in the sense of 1 Introduction to AI: facts and actions written as logic, plus search. The A* search algorithm and the STRIPS planner were both developed for Shakey.

Relationship between AI and robotics

Slide 26

  • AI: intelligence demonstrated by machines, similar to the natural intelligence displayed by humans.
  • Robotics: a branch of engineering that involves the conception, design, manufacture and operation of robots.
  • ROBOT = Sense + Think + Act.
  • Venn diagram: two overlapping circles, Robotics and Artificial Intelligence. Their intersection is labelled artificially intelligent robots.

Slide 27

RoboticsArtificial intelligence
#1 DefinitionIs concerned with the design and operation of robots. Robots are programmed machines that can perform tasks independently or semi-autonomously.AI is an area of computer science that develops systems that can solve issues and help in the same way humans do.
#2 RequirementsNeeds hardware and softwareNeeds software
Common mistake: "robots are AI" or "AI needs a robot"

The Venn diagram has two circles that only partly overlap, on purpose.

  • Robots without AI: a classic factory arm replays a programmed motion very precisely. It senses little and decides nothing, so it is robotics with almost no AI.
  • AI without a robot: a chess engine, a spam filter, an LLM. All the "think" is there, but there is no body and no sensing or acting in the physical world.
  • Both: a self-driving car or a farm robot that recognises weeds needs AI for the think step, because its environment is too messy for fixed rules. That intersection, artificially intelligent robots, is what this programme trains you for.
Why does robotics need hardware and software, but AI only software?

AI's input and output are information: text, images, numbers, decisions. A program on any computer can produce them. A robot's job is to change the physical world, so the sense and act parts of the loop have to be physical devices (sensors, motors, a structure that carries them, power electronics), and software is needed to tie them together. That is why the robotics side of the degree has physics, electronics and mechanics, and the AI side mostly maths and computer science.

Connection: where the two lectures meet

In the terms of 1 Introduction to AI, almost every robot's "think" step is weak AI: task-specific methods such as path planning (symbolic search) or object recognition with deep learning (subsymbolic). The "acting rationally" corner of the AI lecture's 2 × 2 grid (design agents that "do the right thing") is exactly what a robot in the sense–think–act loop does. The Introduction to Robotics course returns to this in 10 Introduction to AI.

Robotics in the curriculum

Core areas of robotics

Left: robotics sits in the intersection of three circles: mechanical, electrical and software. Right (after the arrow), in more detail:

Intuition: reading the diagram as the parts of a robot

Each field is one part of the sense–think–act loop. Mechanical systems are the body: links, joints, gears. Electronic systems are the sensors, motor drivers and power. Computers run the "think" part. Control systems make the actuators follow the commands accurately (feedback). The overlaps are the joints between parts. For example, electro-mechanics is where an electric motor becomes motion, and digital control is the feedback loop running as code on a computer. AI attaches to the computing/control side because it supplies the decisions. A robot fails if any one of these fails. That is why the degree can't be "just programming".

Intuition: localisation, state estimation, SLAM

These words recur in the specialisation and in the research groups below. State estimation means working out the robot's current state (position, orientation, speed) from noisy sensor readings. This is the "compute present state" box in the sense–think–act diagram. Localisation is the special case "where am I on a known map?". SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping) means building the map of an unknown place while locating yourself in it.

Department of Smart Systems Technologies

Control of Networked Systems: Prof. Stephan Weiss, Assoc. Prof. Jan Steinbrener (sst.aau.at/cns)

  • Key research areas: collaborative mobile robot autonomy in 3D space; state-estimation-aware control and motion planning; on-board environment perception and decision making; long-term task execution in changing environments; networked motion generation for multiple agents.
  • Selected projects: autonomous ship inspection with heterogeneous swarms of aerial, crawling and underwater robots (H2020); MEDUSE: multisensor fusion based on equivariant filter design for resilient autonomous aerial navigation; vision-based object-relative navigation of aerial vehicles for powerline inspection (FFG); collaborative state estimation for autonomous fork-lift operation and payload-relative navigation (FFG).

Sensors, Actuators, Modular Robotics: Prof. Hubert Zangl (sst.aau.at/sat)

  • Key research areas: proximity and tactile perception, grasping sensors; real-time sensor simulation (sim2real/digital twins): capacitive, radar, ToF (camera), US, IR, magnetic; sensor design, signal processing and optimisation; self-sustained (autarkic), ultra-low-power wireless sensors; ubiquitous sensing (USE lab, Silicon Austria Labs); human–robot interaction; modular robotics (Prof. Michael Hofbaur).
  • Selected projects: collaborative human–robot workspace (KWF/EFRE); modular multi-modal proximity and tactile perception skin (KWF/EFRE); electromagnetic near-field enhanced UAV landing (FFG); airborne data collection and resilient architectures (ECSEL); load balancing and increasing efficiency by status detection of networked cooling devices (FFG).

Transportation Informatics: Prof. Kyandoghere Kyamakya, Assoc. Prof. Jean Chamberlain Chedjou (sst.aau.at/tig)

  • Key research areas: systems modelling and simulation; advanced deep-learning technologies in transportation (cellular/recurrent neural networks, graph neural networks, autoencoders, generative models, physics-informed neural networks); nonlinear dynamics in intelligent transportation and logistics systems; neurocomputing for various data-analytics applications; neurocomputing for solving inverse problems.
  • Selected projects: neurocomputing-based traffic control and traffic-light state forecast (SWARCO/FFG); AI-based automated document classification (UNIQUARE/FFG); anomaly detection and forecasting in AAL (P.SYS/FFG); AI-based topology extraction in complex analog circuits (INFINEON); robust time-series analysis and forecasting (TIG/OEAD); robust emotion and stress detection for assistance systems; neurocomputing (CeNN, GAN, GNN, PINN) based ultrafast solvers for differential equations (TIG/OEAD/EU-ERASMUS+).
  • Figure: "physics-informed machine learning" as an umbrella linking NN training and in-car AI.

Department of Networked and Embedded Systems

Mobile Systems: Prof. Dr. Christian Bettstetter

  • Key research areas: mobile communications; self-organising systems; multi-drone systems.
  • Selected projects: interference dynamics in wireless networks (FWF); self-organising sync with stochastic coupling (FWF); networked autonomous aerial vehicles (Karl Popper Kolleg); drone communications over 5G networks (T-Mobile); wireless sensor networks for aircraft (Airbus); UWB industrial sensor networks (FFG: Messfeld, Dewesoft); cooperative spatial diversity (Orange); access for cabin transport systems (SKIDATA).

Smart Grids: Prof. Dr. Wilfried Elmenreich

  • Key research areas: smart microgrids; energy informatics; self-organising systems; non-intrusive load monitoring; energy management; photovoltaic systems.
  • Selected projects: energy monitoring: load disaggregation; MONERGY: ICT solutions for energy saving in smart homes; CPSwarm: swarm approach to cyber-physical systems.

Pervasive Computing: Prof. Dr. Bernhard Rinner

  • Key research areas: smart cameras; sensor networks; multi-drone systems; security and privacy protection; self-organising computing systems.
  • Selected projects: trustworthy sensing in visual sensor networks (KWF/FWF); joint doctorate in interactive and cognitive environments (EU); progressing towards secure and cooperating smart cameras (FFG); networked autonomous aerial vehicles (Karl Popper Kolleg); Engineering Proprioception in Computing Systems (EU).

Embedded Communication Systems: Prof. Dr. Andrea M. Tonello

  • Key research areas: power line communications; wireless communications; radio localisation and navigation; statistical signal processing; measurements and HW prototyping; energy management; IoT applications, smart grid and smart mobility; 5G.
  • Selected projects: smart car: electronics and systems in the electric car for sustainable mobility; smart grid: ICT solutions for energy savings in smart homes, smart metering technologies; future networks: convergent gigabit home networks.
